text: The Bell UH-1 Iroquois, commonly known as the "Huey," is a utility military helicopter designed and manufactured by Bell Helicopter. It is the first model in the Huey family and the first turbine-powered helicopter to enter U.S. military service. Development began in the early 1950s, driven by a U.S. Army requirement for a medical evacuation and utility helicopter. The Bell 204, first flown on 20 October 1956, was praised for its single turboshaft engine, outperforming piston-engine helicopters. An initial production contract for 100 HU-1As was signed in March 1960. In response to power limitations, Bell developed improved models; the prototype used a Lycoming YT53-L-1 engine producing 700 shaft horsepower (520 kW), while by 1966, the Lycoming T53-L-13 engine, capable of 1,400 shaft horsepower (1,000 kW), was installed on some variants. A stretched version, first flown in August 1961, was developed to carry more troops, featuring a 41-inch (104 cm) extended fuselage with seating for 15, including crew, and the ability to carry six stretchers and a medic. Modifications included all-aluminium construction, a rotor brake, and alternative powerplants. The Iroquois first saw combat in the Vietnam War in March 1962, serving in roles such as general support, cargo transport, aeromedical evacuation, search and rescue, electronic warfare, and ground attack. Armed gunships were equipped with rockets, grenade launchers, and machine guns and were frequently modified in the field. The U.S. Air Force used Iroquois for reconnaissance, psychological warfare, and support missions in Vietnam, as did the Royal Australian Air Force. Approximately 7,000 Iroquois were deployed in Vietnam, with over 3,300 believed destroyed. The helicopter also saw combat in the Rhodesian Bush War, Falklands War, War in Afghanistan, and the 2007 Lebanon conflict. Originally designated HU-1, the nickname "Huey" became widely used and persisted even after the official redesignation to UH-1 in 1962. Derivatives include the Bell AH-1 Cobra attack helicopter, the Bell 204 and 205 for civilian use, the twin-engine UH-1N Twin Huey developed in the late 1960s, the four-blade Bell 412 introduced in Canada but not the U.S., and the UH-1Y Venom developed in the early 21st century for the U.S. Marine Corps. In U.S. Army service, the Iroquois was phased out in the early 21st century by the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk and Eurocopter UH-72 Lakota, though hundreds remained in service over 50 years after introduction. More than 16,000 Iroquois have been built since 1960. New orders from Japan and the Czech Republic have kept production active. Several countries, including Canada, Germany, Taiwan, Japan, and Italy, have produced the helicopter under license. Operators are found worldwide in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Pacific. In 1952, the U.S. Army sought a new helicopter for MEDEVAC, instrument training, and general utility, noting existing models were too large, underpowered, or complex. In November 1953, revised requirements were submitted. Twenty companies submitted designs, including Bell with the Model 204 and Kaman with a turbine-powered H-43. On 23 February 1955, the Army selected Bell to build three Model 204s for evaluation, designated XH-40. The XH-40, powered by the Lycoming YT53-L-1 engine producing 700 shp (520 kW), first flew on 20 October 1956 at Fort Worth, Texas, with Floyd Carlson at the controls. The Army ordered six YH-40 service test helicopters before the first flight, and two additional prototypes were completed in 1957. In 1959, Bell received a production contract for 182 aircraft, designated HU-1A and named Iroquois after Native American nations. The nickname "Huey" derived from the HU-1 designation became so popular that Bell began casting it on the anti-torque pedals. Even after the official designation changed to UH-1 in 1962 under a unified Department of Defense system, the nickname remained in common use. Army reports found the early YH-40 underpowered with the T53-L-1A engine producing 770 shp (570 kW), prompting the development of the UH-1B with a Lycoming T53-L-5 engine producing 960 shp (720 kW) and a longer cabin for seven passengers or four stretchers and a medic. Testing began in November 1960, with first deliveries in March 1961. In 1960, Bell developed the UH-1C to correct aerodynamic issues in the armed UH-1B, using a 1,100 shp (820 kW) T53-L-11 engine and a new rotor system to improve maneuverability and speed. A new tail boom with a wider vertical fin and larger synchronized elevators was designed. A dual hydraulic control system and improved inlet filter were added for Southeast Asian conditions. Fuel capacity increased to 242 US gallons (920 L), gross weight to 9,500 lb (4,309 kg), and useful load to 4,673 lb (2,120 kg). Production began in June 1966, with 766 units built, including five for the Royal Australian Navy and five for Norway. The Model 205 prototype flew on 16 August 1961, with seven pre-production aircraft delivered to Edwards AFB in March 1961. The 205 initially used a 44-foot (13 m) rotor and T53-L-9 engine with 1,100 shp, later lengthened to 48 feet (15 m) with a 21-inch (53 cm) chord and a longer tail boom, resulting in a gross weight of 9,500 lb (4,309 kg). The Army ordered production in 1963 with the T53-L-11 engine for multi-fuel capability; prototypes were designated YUH-1D and production models UH-1D. In 1966, the UH-1H was introduced with the 1,400 shp (1,000 kW) T53-L-13 engine, and the pitot tube was moved from the nose to the roof of the cockpit to prevent damage during landing. In 1962, the U.S. Marine Corps selected the UH-1B to replace the Cessna O-1 and Kaman OH-43D, resulting in the UH-1E, modified with all-aluminium construction, Marine-compatible radios, a rotor brake for shipboard use, and a roof-mounted rescue hoist. The UH-1E first flew on 7 October 1963, with deliveries starting on 21 February 1964; 192 units were built. Due to production constraints, two versions were produced under the UH-1E designation: the first 34 used the T53-L-11 engine, and later units benefited from UH-1C upgrades. The Marine Corps later upgraded UH-1E engines to the T53-L-13 producing 1,400 shp (1,000 kW). The U.S. Air Force selected a version with the General Electric T58 turboshaft engine for missile base support, requiring a separate offset gearbox due to the rear-mounted T58 output shaft. The UH-1N Twin Huey (Bell 212), developed for Canada in 1968 with a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6T twin-engine set, was also adopted by the U.S. Marine Corps and Navy, with first deliveries in 1971. In 1996, the U.S. Marine Corps launched the H-1 upgrade program, leading to the development of the UH-1Y and AH-1Z variants. The UH-1Y features a lengthened cabin, four-blade rotor, and two more powerful GE T700 engines and entered service in 2008. The Bell 412 is a four-blade version of the twin-engined Bell 212, not adopted by the U.S., but selected by Canada (CH-146 Griffon), licensed in Italy as the Augusta-Bell AB412, and planned for Japan by Subaru. It is a popular commercial and military helicopter and competed in the early 2000s Army Light Utility Helicopter program, losing to the UH-72 Lakota, which replaced aging UH-1 and OH-58A/C models in U.S. National Guard units. The UH-1 has a semi-monocoque metal fuselage with tubular landing skids and two rotor blades. Early models used a single Lycoming T53 turboshaft engine with power ratings from 700 to 1,400 shp (520 to 1,040 kW), while later models often featured twin engines and four-blade rotors. All UH-1 family members share similar construction. The UH-1H is the most-produced version and represents the family. The main structure includes two longitudinal main beams under the cabin, separated by transverse bulkheads, supporting the cabin, landing gear, fuel tanks, transmission, engine, and tail boom. The beams are joined at the lift beam, a short aluminum girder attached to the transmission via a lift link and cargo hook at the center of gravity. Steel lift beams were later introduced due to cracking on high-time airframes. The semi-monocoque tail boom attaches to the fuselage with four bolts. Dynamic components include the engine, transmission, rotor mast, main rotor blades, tail rotor driveshaft, and 42-degree and 90-degree gearboxes for the tail rotor. The main rotor transmission includes a 90-degree bevel gear with a 2.14:1 ratio, followed by a two-stage planetary gearset with a 9.53:1 ratio (3.087:1 each), and an engine output gearbox with a 3.19:1 ratio, resulting in 324 rpm at the main rotor. The two-bladed, semi-rigid rotor design, with pre-coned and underslung blades, is derived from early Bell models like the Bell 47, sharing features such as a damped stabilizer bar. The two-blade system reduces storage space but increases vibration, producing the characteristic "Huey thump" sound, especially during descent and turns. The tail rotor is driven from the main transmission via directional gearboxes, operating at approximately six times the main rotor speed. The UH-1H includes a synchronized elevator on the tail boom linked to the cyclic control, allowing a wider center of gravity range. The standard fuel system has five interconnected tanks, three behind the transmission and two under the cabin floor. The landing gear consists of two arched cross tubes joining skid tubes, with replaceable sacrificial skid shoes. Skis and inflatable floats can be fitted. While the five main fuel tanks are self-sealing, the UH-1H was not factory-armed, though armored pilot seats were available. Internal seating includes two pilot seats and up to 13 passengers or crew, with a maximum configuration of a four-man bench seat.

The UH-1H produces the characteristic 'Huey thump' sound during flight, especially during descent and turning, due to the tail rotor being driven from the main transmission via two directional gearboxes that provide a tail rotor speed approximately six times that of the main rotor to enhance its effectiveness. It features a synchronized elevator on the tail boom linked to the cyclic control, enabling a wider center of gravity range. The standard fuel system includes five interconnected fuel tanks—three mounted behind the transmission and two under the cabin floor—each of which is self-sealing, though the UH-1H was not factory-armed, with armored pilot seats available. Internal seating includes two pilot seats and up to 13 passengers or crew, arranged in a four-man bench seat behind the pilot seats, a five-man bench seat in front of the transmission, and two two-man bench seats on either side, all constructed with aluminum tube frames and canvas seats that are quickly removable and reconfigurable. The cabin can be fitted with up to six stretchers, an internal rescue hoist, auxiliary fuel tanks, spotlights, or other mission kits, and access is via two aft-sliding doors and two forward-hinged panels, which may be removed or pinned open; pilot access is through individual hinged doors. The UH-1H has dual conventional controls with a single hydraulic system boosting the cyclic stick, collective lever, and anti-torque pedals; the collective levers have integral throttles used only for engine start and shutdown, not rotor rpm control, which is automatically governed, while the cyclic and collective control main rotor pitch via push-pull tube linkages to the swashplate, and the anti-torque pedals adjust tail rotor pitch via a tensioned cable arrangement; some UH-1Hs were modified to replace tail rotor control cables with push-pull tubes like the UH-1N Twin Huey. The HU-1A (later UH-1A) first entered service with the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, the 82nd Airborne Division, and the 57th Medical Detachment, with Hueys from the 57th Medical Detachment arriving in South Vietnam in March 1962; the UH-1 has become one of the world's most recognized helicopters due to its role in U.S. involvement in Southeast Asia, particularly Vietnam, where primary missions included general support, air assault, cargo transport, aeromedical evacuation, search and rescue, electronic warfare, and later ground attack. A larger version based on the Model 205 was initially designated the UH-1D and flew operationally from 1963; the first batch of 77 UH-1Ds arrived in South Vietnam in April 1965. UH-1B/C gunships were replaced by the AH-1 Cobra from 1967 to late 1968 due to increasing North Vietnamese anti-aircraft defenses making continued use of UH-1 gunships impractical, after which the Cobra became the Army's primary attack helicopter. UH-1 gunships were often called "Frogs" or "Hogs" when equipped with rockets and "Cobras" or "Guns" when armed with machine guns; troop transport UH-1s were called "Slicks" due to the absence of weapons pods, though they had door gunners and were used in troop transport and medevac roles. UH-1s flew hunter-killer teams with observation helicopters such as the Bell OH-58A Kiowa and Hughes OH-6 Cayuse (Loach); during the 1972 Easter Offensive, two UH-1B helicopters with the XM26 Armament Subsystem were deployed to counter the invasion, with pilots receiving brief crash courses and successfully hitting 151 of 162 fired TOW missiles, including two tanks; these airborne TOW launchers were known as "Hawks Claws" and were based at Camp Holloway. During the Vietnam War, 7,013 UH-1s served in Vietnam, of which 3,305 were destroyed, and 1,151 pilots and 1,231 other crew members were killed. Post-Vietnam, the U.S. Army continued to operate large numbers of UH-1s, using them in combat during the invasions of Grenada (1983), Panama (1989), and the Gulf War (1991), where over 400 Iroquois performed missions, accumulating 31,000 flight hours over nine months with a 70% mission-capable rate, comprising over 20% of all coalition rotorcraft and recording 21% of total flying hours; more than 2,800 UH-1s remained in inventory, with 389 UH-1Vs making up 76% of Army medevac aircraft. Plans to phase out the UH-1 began as early as 1992, with the UH-1 being phased out starting in the 1980s via the introduction of the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk, though the Army UH-1 Residual Fleet retained around 700 units until 2015, primarily for training at Fort Rucker and in selected National Guard units; Army support ended in 2004, and the UH-1 was retired from active Army service in early 2005. Army National Guard retirements accelerated in 2009 with the introduction of the Eurocopter UH-72 Lakota; in 2009, the Guard marked 50 years of Huey service and 40 years with the National Guard with a ceremonial end to service; final flights occurred in Washington, D.C. in 2011 and Pennsylvania in 2010; the final U.S. Army UH-1 was retired in late 2016 and transferred to a state police department. The Huey remains in service with other Armed Forces, with the Air Force UH-1N still in service as of 2024 and scheduled for replacement; on 24 September 2018, the Boeing/Leonardo MH-139 won the competition to replace the UH-1N fleet, with the UH-1N fleet in service as of 2025. The U.S. Navy acquired surplus UH-1B helicopters from the Army, modifying them into gunships known as Seawolves for use with Navy Helicopter Attack (Light) (HA(L)-3), and also acquired UH-1C helicopters in the 1970s; Seawolves operated with Navy river patrol units. After HA(L)-3 was disestablished in 1972, the Navy established two new Naval Reserve Helicopter Attack (Light) Squadrons in 1976: HA(L)-5, the "Blue Hawks," at Naval Air Station Point Mugu in June 1977, and HA(L)-4, the "Red Wolves," at Naval Air Station Norfolk in July 1976. The last regular Navy Huey HH-1 search and rescue helicopters were retired in 2009 and replaced by H-60 Seahawks, and the last Marine Corps UH-1N was retired in 2014. The DEA used UH-1Hs, initially borrowed from the Army, for operations such as Operation Snowcap in Latin America and conducted counter-narcotics raids in Afghanistan, including a July 2009 raid that led to the arrest of an Afghan Border Police commander. Nine Argentine Army Aviation UH-1Hs and two Argentine Air Force Bell 212s were deployed during the Falklands War, performing general transport and SAR missions based at Port Stanley; two were destroyed and the remainder captured by British forces, with three surviving as museum pieces in England and the Falklands. The Royal Australian Air Force operated the UH-1H until 1989, with No. 9 Squadron deploying to South Vietnam in mid-1966 with M60 door guns; four helicopters were converted to gunships known as 'Bushrangers' with two fixed forward-firing M134 7.62 mm miniguns and 7-round rocket pods on each side, and aircrew armed with twin M60 flexible mounts; No. 35 and No. 5 Squadrons also operated the Iroquois through the 1970s and 1980s, contributing to the Multinational Force and Observers in Sinai from 1982 to 1986; in 1988, the RAAF began re-equipping with S-70A Blackhawks. In 1989 and 1990, the RAAF's UH-1Hs were transferred to the 171st Aviation Squadron in Darwin and the 5th Aviation Regiment in Townsville, following a decision to operate battlefield helicopters under the Australian Army; the last Bell UH-1 was retired on 21 September 2007 in Brisbane, replaced by MRH-90 and Tiger helicopters. The Royal Australian Navy's 723 Squadron operated seven UH-1Bs from 1964 to 1989, with three lost in accidents, and deployed during the Vietnam War as part of the Experimental Military Unit. The Salvadoran Air Force operated numerous UH-1s, becoming the largest and most experienced combat helicopter force in Central and South America during the 1980s, fighting for over a decade.

In 1989 and 1990, the Royal Australian Air Force's UH-1H Iroquois were transferred to the 171st Aviation Squadron in Darwin, Northern Territory, and the 5th Aviation Regiment in Townsville, Queensland, following the decision that all battlefield helicopters would be operated by the Australian Army. On 21 September 2007, the Australian Army retired its last Bell UH-1 helicopters, with the final flight occurring in Brisbane, and these were replaced by MRH-90 medium helicopters and Tiger armed reconnaissance helicopters. The Royal Australian Navy's 723 Squadron operated seven UH-1Bs from 1964 to 1989, with three lost in accidents during that period, and deployed Iroquois aircraft and personnel as part of the Experimental Military Unit during the Vietnam War. The Salvadoran Air Force operated numerous UH-1s, becoming the largest and most experienced combat helicopter force in Central and South America during the 1980s, fighting in the Salvadoran Civil War for over a decade and having been trained by the US Army in Vietnam-era tactics; by early 1985, El Salvador had 33 UH-1s in its inventory, some configured as gunships and others as transports, with further expansion supported by US government assistance. Several Salvadoran UH-1M and UH-1H helicopters were modified to carry bombs instead of rocket pods, enabling the military to avoid ground routes vulnerable to guerrilla ambushes, with gunships used to suppress hostile forces ahead of troop insertions. Dornier constructed 352 UH-1Ds under license between 1967 and 1981 for the West German Bundeswehr, which served with both the German Army and Air Force in utility and search and rescue (SAR) roles; after being replaced by twin-engine Eurocopter EC145s, the last UH-1Ds were withdrawn on 12 April 2021. Israel retired its UH-1s in 2002 after 33 years of service, replacing them with Sikorsky UH-60 Blackhawk helicopters, with an initial batch of 10 delivered in 1994; some were passed to pro-Israeli militias in Lebanon, while eleven UH-1Ds were reportedly sold to a Singapore-based logging company but were instead delivered in October 1978 to the Rhodesian Air Force to circumvent a United Nations embargo during the Rhodesian Bush War. In 1960, Subaru agreed to produce the HU-1B for Japan, renamed UH-1B in 1962, along with the HU-1H, renamed UH-1H, and Bell and Subaru developed the UH-1J. Starting in 1993, 130 UH-1Js were produced by Fuji for the Japanese Self-Defense Force. In 2005, two Japan Ground Self-Defense Force (JGSDF) UH-1s were deployed to Pakistan for earthquake relief, and in 2010, after floods, UH-1s were again deployed to assist in disaster relief; Japanese UH-1s have also been used periodically for water bombing against fires. Following the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, Japan's UH-1 fleet was extensively deployed for disaster relief and conducted reconnaissance flights over the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant carrying radiation detection equipment. By the early 2020s, Japan's Acquisition, Technology & Logistics Agency was planning to replace the remaining UH-1s in the JGSDF with a locally-built twin-engine multirole Bell 412, designated the H-2 in JSDF service; the first flight of the Subaru UH-2 occurred in 2022. During the early 1990s, the Lebanese Air Force inducted its first UH-1 helicopters; during the 2007 Lebanon conflict at the Battle of Nahr el-Bared, the Lebanese Army modified several UH-1Hs to carry 500 lb (227 kg) Mark 82 bombs, installing special mounting points on the sides for these high-explosive weapons to strike militant-held positions. After the 2020 Beirut explosion, UH-1s participated in disaster response and were used to extinguish fires. The fleet typically performs search and rescue, troop transport, aerial firefighting, and utility missions; in the late 2010s, specially modified UH-1Ds participated in the first LIDAR mapping exercise in Lebanon, and in February 2021, three additional Bell UH-1H-IIs were delivered to the LAF to augment its fleet. The Royal New Zealand Air Force operated 13 Iroquois with No. 3 Squadron, with the first five UH-1Ds delivered in 1966, nine UH-1Hs in 1970, and one more UH-1H in 1976; all UH-1D aircraft were upgraded to 1H specification during the 1970s, and two ex-US Army UH-1H airframes were purchased in 1996, with three lost in accidents. The RNZAF retired the Iroquois, replacing them with NHIndustries NH90 helicopters, with eight active NH90s and one spare procured; the process was initially expected by the end of 2013 but was delayed until 2016, with aircraft retired as they reached their next major group servicing intervals; the UH-1H was retired as the NH90 fleet stood up. On 21 May 2015, the remaining six UH-1H helicopters conducted a final tour before their planned retirement on 1 July, marking 49 years of service in areas including the UK, Southeast Asia, Timor, the Solomon Islands, various South Pacific nations, and the Antarctic. One UH-1 was preserved at the New Zealand National Museum after retirement in 2013, delivered in 2015, having entered service in 1966. During the 1973 Pakistan floods, the US sent six UH-1H helicopters, operating mainly in southern Pakistan, which were later left at Dhamial and then gifted to Pakistan by the US government following a proposal to Prime Minister Bhutto before his 1974 state visit. The Philippine Air Force (PAF) acquired Bell UH-1s, receiving the first in March 1969, with a unit reorganized into the 205th Tactical Helicopter Wing; the first four helicopters (tail numbers 290–293) were factory-new, with US Army production beginning just two years prior. In PAF service, the Hueys were used to combat insurgents and conduct disaster relief after earthquakes and typhoons; following this, the PAF armed them with M-60 machine guns, with aircrew undergoing gunnery training at Fort Magsaysay in February 1971, and the enhanced firepower was demonstrated in punitive operations at Barrio Talbac, San Ildefonso, Bulacan, on 7–8 April 1971, during which Huk Commander Beto and his aide Yoyong were killed. Francis Ford Coppola filmed Apocalypse Now in the Philippines, using Philippine Hueys for the iconic scene with Robert Duvall as Lt. Colonel Kilgore, due to President Ferdinand Marcos's agreement. In 2004, the PAF procured 20 refurbished UH-1H helicopters from Singapore Technologies Aerospace (ST Aero) for $12 million. In 2013, due to urgent operational needs, the PAF procured new Bell 412 units delivered in 2015; it also acquired 21 refurbished Bell UH-1D units with Night Vision Compatible Cockpit under a PHP1.26bn ($28 million) contract with Rice Aircraft Services and Eagle Copters joint venture, delivered in 2015. In October 2019, the Philippines made a deal with Japan to acquire spare parts to restore seven stored UH-1s to flightworthy condition. By January 2021, the PAF had 13 UH-1H and 10 UH-1D helicopters in operational service. In 2021, a plan to retire all remaining UH-1s was raised after a series of crashes; on 14 October 2021, the PAF officially decommissioned its UH-1D fleet, with retired aircraft stored at Clark Air Base, though airworthy airframes were returned to service due to lack of aircraft. The UH-1's role is now being fulfilled by recently delivered Poland-built PZL Mielec (Sikorsky S-70i) helicopters acquired under a Multi-Year Contractual Authority (MYCA); in January 2022. In 2022, the Philippines announced that some retired Hueys would be reactivated with Turkish company ASFAT's assistance, and Japan planned to donate UH-1s from its service to the Philippine Army; Japan is introducing new Hueys as replacements. As of December 2024, twenty-three units are in active service. Very late in the Rhodesian Bush War, the Rhodesian Air Force obtained 11 former Israeli Agusta-Bell 205As in violation of sanctions, allegedly using intermediaries to evade them; locally known as Cheetahs, these were restored to flightworthy condition and assigned to No. 8 Squadron, functioning as armed gunships and troop transports; one Cheetah was lost in combat in September 1979 after being hit by an RPG over Mozambique, and at least three other UH-1s were lost; the surviving helicopters were put up for sale in 1990. In July 2009, Yemen received four UH-1Hs, which remained grounded for most of their service, with at least one heavily damaged during Saudi-led airstrikes on Al Daylami and Al Anad Air Bases. In U.S. service, the G, J, Q, R, S, T, W, and Z model designations are used by the AH-1; the UH-1 and AH-1 are considered members of the same H-1 series, and the military does not use I (India) or O (Oscar) for aircraft designations to avoid confusion with "one" and "zero" respectively. Data from Jane's All the World's Aircraft 1987-88 is cited. The image of American troops disembarking from a Huey became an iconic image of the Vietnam War, appearing in films such as The Green Berets, The Deer Hunter, Platoon, Hamburger Hill, Apocalypse Now, Casualties of War, and Born on the Fourth of July, and prominently in We Were Soldiers, which depicts the Battle of Ia Drang. Author Robert Mason recounts his career as a UH-1 "Slick" pilot in his memoir, Chickenhawk. The 2002 journey of Huey 091, displayed in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, is detailed in the 2004 documentary In the Shadow of the Blade.
